title: seva as vocation
hook: jobs are handed out for a king's great sacrifice, and the guest of honor takes the one at the guests' feet

segments.voice: Yesterday, seva as vocation was Rantideva at his table: the same honor for every guest, down to the last cup of water. Whom did you serve that you'd usually walk past? Day one thousand two hundred eleven.
screen: `THE SAME HONOR FOR EVERY GUEST.` · `JOBS AT A GREAT FEAST.`

segments.voice: A great royal sacrifice is underway, and someone has to hand out the jobs. King Yudhishthira is holding the Rajasuya, the rite that marks a king as sovereign, and kings and sages have come from everywhere. There are crowds to feed, gifts to give, money to guard, elders to look after. So everyone pitches in, the way families do before a big wedding. Each one gets a job. And Krishna, the guest this same story has the assembly honor first, has a job too. The Bhagavata's tenth book tells you which one, almost in passing.
screen: `A KING'S GREAT SACRIFICE.` → `EVERYONE GETS A JOB.` → `WHICH JOB DOES KRISHNA TAKE?`

segments.voice: Here's the Bhagavata's list. Bhima ran the kitchen. Duryodhana kept the treasury. Sahadeva received the guests, Nakula gathered supplies, and Arjuna looked after the elders. Draupadi served the food. Karna handed out the gifts. And Krishna washed the feet of the guests. Sit with that. In this same story, the assembly gives Krishna the first honor of the whole ceremony. For his devotees, he is God. And his job is at the guests' feet, with water, washing off the dust of the road. In tradition, water for a guest's feet is part of the welcome. It's also work done kneeling. He does it anyway, and the text mentions it in passing, inside a list, as though nothing could be more natural. For a vocation of seva, that short list does two things. First, it shows that every job at the feast was service. The treasury and the kitchen, the gifts and the plates: nobody on that list was there just to be seen. Second, it shows that the job doesn't measure the person. The one honored first worked at the feet. On an ordinary Tuesday, that means the trash bags, the folding chairs, the person stuck at the sign-in table: those aren't lesser roles in this picture. In the Bhagavata, that's where Krishna stands.
screen: `KITCHEN, TREASURY, GUESTS, GIFTS.` · `KRISHNA WASHES THE GUESTS' FEET.` · `HONORED FIRST, KNEELING AT THEIR FEET.` · `THE JOB DOESN'T MEASURE THE PERSON.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: take the job nobody reaches for. Settle, and breathe. Think of a place you'll be this week where things need doing: home, work, a temple, a family gathering. Notice which job you'd naturally reach for, and which one you'd hope someone else takes. Hold that second job in mind. Picture yourself doing it gladly, with nobody noticing. If you pray, you can offer that unchosen work to the One you pray to. The bell holds the time.
Seva as vocation. Service as a life's work: at Yudhishthira's sacrifice every job is service, and the guest of honor washes feet. Today's word.
Your line: seva as vocation. Today, quietly take the job nobody wants, and do it as if for an honored guest. Day one thousand two hundred eleven.

howItsDone: At Hindu temple festivals and family ceremonies, volunteers take on the cooking, serving, cleaning and welcoming as seva, and stories like Krishna washing guests' feet at the Rajasuya are told to honor that work.

fork.setup: you're Krishna at Yudhishthira's great sacrifice. the assembly has just honored you first. jobs are being handed out. which do you take?
fork.reveal: Krishna washes the guests' feet. the one honored first takes the job at their feet, and the text reports it in passing.

original.note: Sanskrit: the royal consecration rite that marks a king as sovereign; Yudhishthira's Rajasuya is the setting.

trapdoor: what you thought: the greater the person, the grander the job.
what it means: at Yudhishthira's sacrifice every job is service, and the one honored first washes feet.
what a scholar hears: Bhagavata Purana 10.75.4–7, the duties at the Rajasuya, with Krishna at the washing of feet, read after the first honor given him in 10.74.

sources.ref: Bhagavata Purana 10.74 (the Rajasuya; the assembly gives Krishna the first honor)

Bhagavata Purana 10.75.4–7 (the duties: Bhima the kitchen, Duryodhana the treasury, Sahadeva receiving guests, Nakula supplies, Arjuna serving elders, Krishna washing feet, Draupadi serving food, Karna giving gifts)

notes: Confirm the list of duties and its verse numbers (10.75.4–7), especially Krishna's task (washing the feet of guests) and the assignments of Sahadeva, Nakula and Arjuna.
'Water for a guest's feet is part of the old Hindu welcome' refers to padya among the traditional offerings to a guest; not stated in the cited text. Confirm or cut.
'The text mentions it in a single line' describes the Bhagavata's brevity here; confirm.
The Mahabharata's own account of the Rajasuya (Sabha Parva) differs in detail; only the Bhagavata is cited.
howItsDone is a general description of festival volunteering; confirm wording.

Editor pass: removed 'at the door' (the text doesn't place the foot-washing there) from hook, teach, screen, practice and fork; removed the sequence claims 'has just chosen to honor first' and 'chose' (10.74 and 10.75 don't establish that order or that Krishna chose the task); 'every cousin' and 'the family' dropped, since Karna and Krishna aren't simply cousins of the hosts; 'a single line' became 'in passing'; 'old Hindu welcome' became 'in tradition'; 'the dishes' became 'the trash bags' to avoid echoing day 1200's sink.
